This verse recalls the favours given to Solomon, son of David: the jinn worked for him as he wished, building lofty structures called 'mahareeb', which the commentators understand in different ways. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take them as fine buildings, al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi as palaces or mosques, while Mujahid says they were lesser than palaces and Ibn Zayd that they were dwellings. The jinn also made statues ('tamathil') of copper, glass or marble, enormous basins (jifan) like watering troughs, and huge fixed cooking pots that could not be moved. The verse then commands the family of David to act in gratitude, and notes that few of God's servants are truly grateful. The commentators agree that gratitude is shown through the heart, the tongue and deeds, with prayer and obedience as its chief forms. Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that David divided the hours of night and day among his household for worship. On the statues, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan record that some scholars held such images permitted in Solomon's law and abrogated in the law of Muhammad, while others rejected that reading and held that the prohibition was always in force. Al-Razi observes that the verse teaches that true gratitude for such blessings is beyond human capacity, so that the effort itself is a form of thanks.

This verse tells of the death of the Prophet Solomon, peace be upon him. The commentators explain that God decreed his death while he stood leaning on his staff in his place of worship, and the jinn continued their arduous labours, believing him alive and unaware of his death. The exegetes agree that the 'creature of the earth' is the termite, a small insect that gnaws wood, and that its eating of the staff caused Solomon to fall. Only then did the jinn learn of his death, and it became clear to people that the jinn do not know the unseen; had they known it, they would have realised he had died and not remained in that humiliating toil. Opinions differ on how long his death went unnoticed: some report a full year, while Ibn Kathir considers the narration on this point strange and its attribution to the Prophet unsound, noting that it derives partly from the traditions of the People of the Book, so that only what agrees with the truth may be accepted. Al-Tabari and others record variant readings attributed to Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn Abbas that express the same meaning. The readings of the word 'minsa'atahu' vary between a hamza and its absence, and the lexicographers link it to a root meaning to drive away, the staff being used to push things off. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan take the clause introduced by 'that' as an apposition to 'the jinn', the aim being to make plain their inability to know the unseen, and some see in it a note of mockery. Many commentators present the verse as evidence against the claim that the jinn know the unseen.

The commentators explain that this verse concerns the people of Sheba in Yemen, to whom God granted two gardens, one on the right and one on the left of their valley. They were told to eat of their Lord's provision and give Him thanks, for their land was good and their Lord forgiving. There is broad agreement on the extraordinary fertility of the place: according to Ibn Zayd and Qatada, a woman could walk among the trees with a basket on her head and return with it full without touching the fruit, and the land was free of mosquitoes, scorpions and snakes.

As to the name Saba, most commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, take it to be a man, the ancestor of tribes, citing the hadith of Farwa ibn Musayk, whereas others such as Ibn Atiyya take it to be a tribe or a land. The readers differ between the diptote and non-diptote forms and between the singular and plural for 'their dwelling', but most commentators regard the meaning as essentially the same.

The commentators differ on whether the gardens themselves are the sign. Al-Tabari and al-Zamakhshari consider that their story and its lesson are the sign, while al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi see the gardens themselves as proof of God's power. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the two gardens stand for connected groups of orchards rather than just two.

All agree that after the people turned away and refused to give thanks, God sent the flood of al-Arim, which broke the dam, and their gardens became bitter trees and tamarisk. The commentators see this punishment as the due reward of their ingratitude, and note that God requites in this way only the deeply ungrateful, with some divergence on whether this rule is general or specific.

The commentators describe the people of Saba in Yemen, who had been given two great gardens on the right and left of their valley. When they turned away from gratitude to God and rejected His messengers, the dam (sayl al-'arim) that held their water burst, flooding their gardens and wealth. God then replaced their two gardens with two others whose fruit was bitter, where grew the arak tree, the athl (tamarisk-like tree) and a little lote-tree. The interpreters agree that this punishment followed from disbelief and turning away. They differ on what 'arim means: some take it as the dam itself, others as a violent flood, a valley's name, or a rat that gnawed through the dam, a report found in al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi identify khamt with the arak tree and its berries, while al-Zajjaj and al-Mubarrad take it to mean any plant bitter enough to be inedible. Al-Tabari prefers the reading with tanwin. Ibn 'Abbas identifies athl with the tamarisk, while others describe a larger tree of similar kind. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya explain the name 'two gardens' given to the replacements as an ironic figure of speech. On the phrase 'wa-hal nujazi illa al-kafur', Mujahid says that only the disbeliever is punished for all his deeds, while al-Hasan holds that only the great disbeliever receives such a requital. The passage also describes the closely spaced towns between Yemen and Syria, the safe travel, the people's later request for longer distances, and their dispersal, which became a proverb among the Arabs.

The commentators explain that this verse closes the story of the people of Sheba, who had been granted two gardens on either side of their valley and a good land, yet turned away from gratitude and rejected their messengers. God sent upon them the flood of al-Arim, which broke their dam and destroyed their gardens, and replaced them with two gardens bearing bitter fruit, tamarisk, and a few lote trees. The word "that" refers to this change, which the verse presents as a recompense for their disbelief. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read the recompense here as punishment for the one who is deeply ungrateful, a view shared by al-Mawardi and Ibn Atiyya. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari note that the root can mean either reward or punishment, but that here it means punishment. Al-Qurtubi reports Mujahid's view that the believer is rewarded without being punished, and Tawus's view that only the disbeliever is subjected to a strict reckoning; Ibn Juzayy and al-Qasimi take similar lines. On the recitation, al-Farra and Abu Ubayd prefer the first person plural "nujazi" with the accusative "kafur", while the majority reads the passive "yujza" with "kafur" in the nominative. The commentators agree that both readings carry nearly the same meaning.

This verse describes another blessing given to the people of Sheba: God placed between them and the blessed towns, which most commentators identify as the towns of Syria, a chain of settlements so close together that one could be seen from the next. A traveller could rest at midday in one town and spend the night in another, carrying neither provisions nor water. Al-Hasan and Qatada explain that the distance between two towns could be covered in half a day. Ibn Kathir reports that they journeyed in complete safety, without fear of hunger, thirst or enemies. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baghawi take the word zahira to mean adjacent or visible, while Ibn 'Atiyya also suggests it refers to small settlements outside the cities. The commentators agree that the safety was total by night and by day. Yet they asked God to lengthen their journeys. Al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baghawi read this as arrogance and ingratitude for a blessing received, whereas al-Kalbi and Ibn Zayd see a wish for hardship, so that the wealthy could set themselves apart from the poor with mounts and provisions. Al-Razi allows that the request may have been made through the tongue of the situation. All agree that this wrong they did to themselves led to their scattering, so that they became a story and a proverb, dispersed like the hands of Sheba. Al-Sha'bi names the places where they settled, Syria, Yathrib, Tihama and Oman, though Ibn Kathir considers some of these transmissions doubtful.

This verse recounts the request of the people of Saba, who, having grown ungrateful for God's favour, asked that the distances of their journeys be lengthened. Their towns lay so close together between Yemen and Syria that they could travel by night and by day in safety without carrying provisions. According to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, they wanted deserts to cross so they could ride mounts and carry supplies, which amounted to arrogance toward the poor. God then made them into a tale that people repeat and scattered them through the lands. These commentators agree that the blessed towns are those of Syria, and that the story is a lesson for everyone who is patient in trial and grateful in blessing. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Ishaq report that the tribes dispersed: Ghassan to Syria, the Ansar to Yathrib, Khuza'a to Tihama and the Azd to Oman. On the reading, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read the imperative with a doubled 'ayn, most read it with an alif, and Ya'qub reads the past tense, which al-Tabari considers marginal and which Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Atiyya take as complaint or boastfulness. Al-Zamakhshari sees a display of weariness with comfort. As for the words ahadith and mumazzaq, most understand them as dispersal, while Ibn Salam takes them to mean reduction to dust, an interpretation the other commentators regard as unlikely.

This verse reports that Iblis saw his assumption about the children of Adam come true: they followed him, except for a group of believers. The commentators explain that Iblis's assumption rested on what he saw of Adam's weakness before his whisperings, on the desire and anger built into human nature, or on what he heard the angels say about the vicegerent on earth. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read the verb in both forms, showing that both readings are sound, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi explain the lighter and heavier forms through different grammatical paths. On the exception, the views differ. Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd, as cited by al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi, hold that the believers as a whole did not follow him in the core of the faith. Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi note that the word min may be explanatory rather than partitive, and al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi take the group to be the sincere believers who did not follow him in disobedience. Al-Qurtubi reports that some say the verse concerns the people of Sheba only, while others take it to be general. Al-Hasan adds that Iblis had no whip or sword, only promises and delusions. The phrase 'that We may know' is read by the exegetes in two ways: as manifest knowledge that brings reward and punishment, or as the distinction between the believer and the doubter. God is the watchful guardian over all things.

This passage of Surat Saba explains that Iblis had no coercive power or compelling proof over people; his role was limited to calling, adorning evil and whispering. The commentators explain that God gave him this power as a test, so that the one who believes in the Hereafter might be distinguished from the one who doubts it, and that the knowledge meant is manifest knowledge which entails reward, not a new knowledge in God, whose knowledge precedes all things. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi agree that the phrase 'Iblis confirmed his assumption about them' means that his expectation about them came true, since they followed him, except for a group of believers. The readings differ slightly: the light reading makes the assumption a verbal noun or an adverb of time, while the intensive reading makes it an object meaning to make the assumption come true; commentators see both as conveying the same sense. Scholars differ on the exception in 'that We might know': az-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi see it as the reason for the permission granted, whereas Ibn Qutayba and al-Nasafi see it as the manifestation of what was already known. Ibn al-Qayyim and al-Shinqiti regard the exception as disconnected in some respects. As for 'your Lord is Guardian over all things', Ibn Kathir understands it as God's protection of believers against Satan's schemes, while al-Tabari and al-Razi see it as God's all-encompassing knowledge and power. The following verses, discussed by most tafsirs, affirm that the beings invoked besides God own not even an atom's weight, have no share and no helper, and that intercession benefits only by God's permission.

This verse states that the beings the polytheists invoke besides God own not even the weight of an atom in the heavens or on earth, have no share in creation or dominion, and give God no support in governing. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn al-Jawzi, agree that it answers the belief that these powers benefit the idolaters or intercede for them. It therefore denies independent sovereignty, partnership, assistance and intercession, except for one whom God has permitted. Al-Razi and Ibn al-Qayyim note that these four degrees cover everything through which a benefit might be expected, so denying them all cuts off the roots of polytheism. Ibn Kathir also sees a challenge to the idolaters to call upon their gods. According to al-Baghawi and al-Tha'labi, the verse was revealed during the famine that struck the Quraysh, while Ibn 'Atiyya presents it as a test of proof.

The phrase 'until fear is lifted from their hearts' has been read in different ways. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi apply it to the angels, who swoon when they hear the revelation and then, once the fear has gone, ask what their Lord has said and answer: the truth. They rely on the hadith of Abu Hurayra in the Sahih of al-Bukhari. Al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd take it to mean the polytheists at death, who acknowledge the truth when acknowledgement no longer helps them. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi link the phrase to the waiting for permission to intercede.

The commentators agree that intercession happens only by God's permission, and that God is the Most High, the Great.

This verse states that intercession with God benefits no one except those whom God has permitted to intercede, or on whose behalf He has permitted it. The commentators agree that the decision rests with God alone, and that the verse refutes the polytheists' belief that their deities would intercede for them. The phrase "until fear is removed from their hearts" describes a scene in which, after the permission is given, the dread leaves and they ask one another, "What has your Lord said?" They answer, "The truth," for He is the Most High, the Great. Scholars differ on who is meant by those whose hearts are frightened. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi, drawing on numerous hadiths about revelation, take it to be the angels, who are struck with awe when they hear God's speech and then recover; Ibn Kathir considers this the soundest view, as do Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn Juzayy. Others, such as al-Hasan, Ibn Zayd and Mujahid, reported by al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Kathir, hold that the reference is to the polytheists at death or on the Day of Resurrection, when they regain their awareness and acknowledge the truth. Al-Razi offers several interpretations, including the fright of the heavens at the announcement of the Hour. Several commentators also record variant readings of the verb, all of which convey the sense of removing fear.

God commands His Prophet to ask the polytheists who provides for them from the heavens through rain and from the earth through plants, and to answer on their behalf that it is Allah, since they have no other answer. The Prophet then says that one of the two parties, either the believers or the idolaters, is upon guidance or in clear error. This is a fair-minded form of debate that presses the opponent with the argument without openly calling him a liar. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi agree that the believers are upon guidance and the associators in manifest error. Al-Tabari, al-Nasafi and al-Zamakhshari see in this a gentle way of ending obstinacy without a direct verdict. Al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayda hold that (or) means (and), whereas the Basran grammarians keep its proper sense and deny that it expresses doubt. Al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari explain that the choice of (upon) for guidance and (in) for error evokes the image of one who rides high and one who is plunged in darkness. Ibn 'Uthaymin and al-Jaza'iri draw lessons on gentleness toward the opponent and on reasoning by systematic division. Ibn 'Ashur sees in this tone a way of placing the adversary in a position of defeat without imposing it outright.

This verse records that the Prophet ﷺ speaks to the polytheists with courtesy in his argument: each party, he tells them, answers only for its own deeds, so the disbelievers are not held accountable for the sins of the believers, nor the believers for the actions of the disbelievers. The commentators explain that the "crime" attributed to the believers means the minor slips and faults from which no believer is free, while the "deed" attributed to the polytheists means unbelief and the grave sins. The Qur'an thus uses milder words for the believers and stronger ones for their opponents, out of fairness, a subtlety noted by al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi, Abu Hayyan, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi. As for the next phrase, "Our Lord will gather us, then judge between us with truth," al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and others take it to refer to the Day of Resurrection, where God judges justly, the word "fath" meaning judgement. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi specify that this judgement means admitting the righteous to Paradise and the wrongdoers to Hell. Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note that "al-Fattah" means the judge, and that the passage carries a warning and a rebuke. On abrogation, al-Qurtubi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn Juzayy, al-Shawkani and others hold the verse abrogated by the verse of the sword, whereas Ibn 'Ashur argues it does not concern fighting and so is not abrogated; Ibn Kathir does not mention abrogation. Linguistically, al-Farra' and Abu 'Ubayda explain that "aw" sometimes carries the sense of "wa", while others see it as a way of softening the argument by leaving the conclusion implicit.

This verse states that our Lord will gather the Prophet ﷺ and his opponents on the Day of Resurrection, then will judge between them with truth, so that the one who is rightly guided is distinguished from the one who is misguided. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Baydawi, explain the verb "yaftah" as "to judge" or "to decide," and Ibn 'Abbas glosses al-Fattah as "the judge." They conclude that the believers will enter Paradise and the disbelievers the Fire, as al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud state. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi note that this wording is more equitable than the preceding verse, since it assigns the sin to the believers and the deeds to the addressees, with great courtesy. Ibn Kathir adds that this is not meant as doubt but as fairness in debate. Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi hold that these verses were abrogated by the verse of the sword, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Biqa'i do not accept this and read them as a tone of truce. Abu Hayyan notes that the reading of 'Isa, "al-Fatih," is an active participle, while the majority reading "al-Fattah" is an intensive form, and he says the phrase carries a warning and rebuke. Al-Alusi explains that the word fath metaphorically refers to resolving a difficult matter, like opening a closed door.

God commands His Prophet to challenge the polytheists to show him those they have made partners with God. If they showed them, they would find no creation or benefit in them, and God answers with "Kalla", meaning the matter is not as they claim, for true divinity belongs to Allah, the Mighty who overcomes all things and the Wise in His governance. Most commentators, including al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan, understand the verb "show" as meaning "make known", so that the idols are the third object and the polytheists must produce the proof of any partnership. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir stress that the idols have no share with God in creation or power. The context reminds that God is the provider, through rain from heaven and plants from earth, which the polytheists do not deny. Scholars also discuss the particle "or" in "we or you are upon guidance or in clear error": al-Mawardi and al-Baghawi take it as a courteous way of addressing an opponent, Ibn Kathir reads it as a way of declaring one side wrong, and Abu Hayyan notes that it may stand for "and". The verse that follows speaks of the gathering on the Day of Judgement and the just decision of the Knowing Judge.

The commentators explain that this verse affirms the universal mission of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: God sent him to all people, not only to his own tribe. The widely accepted meaning is that he was sent to humankind as a whole, Arabs and non-Arabs, red and black, bringing good news of Paradise to those who obey and warning of the Fire to those who disobey. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Ibn Kathir report this, and Ibn Kathir cites the authentic hadith of Jabir that he was sent to all people, which Ibn 'Atiyya counts among the distinctions granted to him. The word 'kaffatan' has been debated. Al-Zajjaj, al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan take it as a description of the sending, meaning comprehensive or restraining, with the feminine ending adding emphasis; Abu 'Ali al-Farisi, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Radi allow it to qualify 'people', placed first for emphasis, a view al-Zamakhshari rejects. Others read it as general, meaning a sending that encompasses everyone, as al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi do. As for 'but most people do not know', most understand it as their ignorance that he is a prophet or of the true nature of the promise and warning; Ibn Kathir reads it as consolation for the rejection. The shared conclusion is that the verse establishes the general prophethood and that truth is not measured by the number of believers. The passage then turns to the disbelievers asking when the promise will come, and they are told there is a fixed appointed day that can be neither delayed nor advanced.

The verse reports the mocking question of the disbelievers: when will this promise come, if you are truthful? Most commentators, including al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn Kathir, al-Nasafi and Abu al-Su'ud, understand the promise as the Day of Resurrection, while Ibn Juzayy also allows that it may mean the punishment descending on them in this world. The answer given to the Prophet, they agree, is that there is an appointed day from which they cannot delay or hasten by a single moment.

Al-Dahhak, cited by al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi, takes that day to be the moment of death, and al-Qurtubi reports this view along with the view that it is the Day of Badr. Al-Shawkani and Ibn 'Ashur also consider Badr a possibility, and Ibn 'Ashur suggests that those killed that day may have been among those who spoke these words. Al-Alusi holds that the speakers were some of the polytheists of the Prophet's time rather than people in general.

Several scholars, including Ibn 'Ashur, al-Alusi and al-Sha'rawi, observe that calling the Resurrection a "promise", a word normally used for good news, has an ironic tone. Al-Zamakhshari explains that the reply matches the purpose of the question, which was defiance and denial. Al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan note variant readings and grammatical questions around the phrase "mi'ad yawm", though these do not change the general meaning.

This verse answers the disbelievers who mockingly asked when the promised threat would come. God tells His Messenger to say that they have an appointed day from which they cannot delay even an hour, nor hasten it. Most commentators, including Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi, Ibn Juzayy, Ibn Sa'di and Ibn Uthaymin, take this to be the Day of Resurrection, and Ibn Kathir adds that its time is fixed and neither increased nor reduced. Al-Dahhak, as reported by al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi, and al-Qurtubi also mention the moment of death, when each person's term arrives. Abu Hayyan, Ibn Ashur and al-Qurtubi report the view that the day is the Battle of Badr, which had already been a punishment for the unbelievers in this world. Al-Sam'ani says that both the Resurrection and death are valid interpretations. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Abu al-Su'ud explain that the answer is a threat that fits the intent of the questioners, who asked out of obstinacy rather than seeking guidance. Al-Razi adds that the refusal to name a time shows the greatness of the matter, since a trivial request would be met without delay. On grammar, al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi and Abu Hayyan discuss the readings: the construction mi'ad yawm, where the day explains the appointment, and the accusative yawman, which may express magnitude or time. Ibn Sa'di holds that not knowing the timing does not undermine the truth of the message. The commentators agree that the day is certain and cannot be postponed or advanced, but differ on which day is meant.

The verse reports the words of the disbelievers, the polytheists of Mecca, who say they will never believe in this Qur'an or in what came before it. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir, understand 'what is before it' as the Torah, the Gospel and the earlier scriptures and prophets, a reading also given by Qatada, while Ibn 'Atiyya explains that a minority opinion reading it as the Last Day is a mistake, since 'before' means what precedes in time. The verse then describes the wrongdoers standing before their Lord and blaming one another. The weak followers tell the proud leaders that they would have believed had it not been for them. The leaders deny having turned them from guidance after it came and declare that the followers were themselves criminals. The followers answer that the scheming of night and day, by which they were ordered to disbelieve and to set up rivals to God, was the real cause. Al-Farra and al-Mubarrad explain this as a figurative construction, comparable to saying that a night is awake and a day fasting, while Ibn Kathir and Ibn Juzayy take it to mean the leaders' constant plotting by night and by day. Commentators agree that the answer to the conditional 'if you could see' is omitted to heighten the terror, that the shackles around the necks are punishment, and that each is repaid according to deeds. They differ on the verb 'they concealed' the regret: some take it as hiding it and others as displaying it, a double sense Qurtubi illustrates with a line of Imru al-Qays.

This verse records the exchange on the Day of Judgment between the weak followers and the proud leaders who had misled them. The followers say that they would have believed had the leaders not turned them away from guidance. The leaders reply with a denial: we did not turn you away after the guidance had come to you; rather, you were yourselves guilty. The commentators generally read the question as a rhetorical negation, meaning that the disbelief of the followers came from their own choice rather than compulsion. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir present the leaders as disowning responsibility, and Ibn Kathir adds that they offered no proof for their misguidance. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi, Abu Hayyan and Ibn 'Ashur note that placing "we" first denies causation, while "bal" affirms the inherent guilt of the listeners. Ibn 'Atiyya sees the followers' words as a rebuke aimed at their leaders. Ibn Sa'di and Ibn 'Ashur add that the leaders feared being blamed for the whole affair. Later verses are then treated by several commentators: the followers blame the leaders' deceit by night and day, both groups hide or reveal their regret when they see the punishment, and iron collars are placed on the necks of the disbelievers. The commentators do not settle between these readings, but all agree that the recompense corresponds to what people did.

This verse describes the mutual recrimination of the damned on the Day of Judgment. The weak, meaning the followers, accuse the arrogant leaders of having turned them away from faith. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi explain the reply "rather, the scheming of night and day" as your scheming against us by night and by day, the act being attributed to time in a figurative way, as one says "your night is spent standing in prayer and your day in fasting", with a line of Jarir cited in support. Al-Zamakhshari notes that the followers answer by overturning the leaders' denial. Others, such as Ibn Atiyya and al-Qurtubi, report that the scheming also refers to long hope and prolonged security that deceived people. The commentators agree that "andad" means equals or partners, and on the hidden regret: it was concealed out of fear of reproach, according to al-Razi and al-Baydawi, or displayed, the word being for some a term with two opposite meanings, which Ibn Atiyya and others dispute. The "fetters" are for most of them chains binding the hands to the neck; Ibn Kathir applies them to leaders and followers alike. The verse ends by saying they will be repaid only for what they did, a point on which all agree.

God consoles His Prophet Muhammad by explaining that the pattern among earlier nations is the same. Whenever a warner was sent to a town, its affluent leaders, the mutrafun, declared that they disbelieved in what he brought. Al-Tabari, Qatada, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi take them to be the chiefs, the powerful and the ringleaders of evil. Al-Mawardi gives three readings: tyrants, the wealthy, or those enjoying favours, while al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi stress the arrogance that comfort and luxury produce. Most commentators treat the verse as consolation for the Prophet in the face of the rejection by Quraysh's leaders. The verse then reports their boast of wealth and children, which they took as proof that God approves of them and that they would not be punished. According to al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi, God replies that the expansion or restriction of provision is a test, not a sign of approval or anger. The commentators agree that wealth and children do not bring one closer to God, only faith and righteous deeds do, and that the reward is multiplied, according to Ibn Zayd up to tenfold or more. Ibn Kathir cites a report about the occasion of revelation, in which the chiefs rejected the Prophet while the humble followed him.

This verse reports the claim of the wealthy and privileged who rejected the messengers: they boasted of having more wealth and children and said they would never be punished, neither in this world nor in the next, since God would not have given them these riches had He not approved of their religion and deeds. The commentators explain that they judged the afterlife by the conditions of this world. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Nasafi and Abu Hayyan agree that the verse consoles the Prophet, since opposition from the rich to the messengers is a recurring pattern among earlier communities. The divine answer, which most exegetes spell out, is that God expands or restricts provision as a trial, and that this proves neither His pleasure nor His displeasure; most people do not understand this. Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi stress that what brings a person closer to God is faith and righteous action, not possessions. Opinions differ on the promised doubling: Ibn Zayd and Muhammad ibn Ka'b take it to mean the multiplication of good deeds, up to tenfold or more, while others see it simply as an increase; some conclude that wealth combined with piety is a blessing. As for what is spent in God's way, He replaces it, in this life or the next, provided it is spent neither extravagantly nor stingily, according to Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr. The commentators conclude that wealth and poverty in themselves do not determine a person's final fate.

The commentators explain that this verse answers those who thought that wealth in property and children proves God's approval and love. God tells His Prophet ﷺ to say that his Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it to whom He wills, and that this expansion or restriction is a test, not a sign of approval or anger. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Baghawi and al-Baydawi agree that abundance and scarcity rest solely with God's will, that a disbeliever or a disobedient person may be given plenty and a pious believer may be tried with want, and that one therefore cannot infer the fate of the Hereafter from this. Al-Tabari and Ibn al-Jawzi note that most people do not grasp this wisdom and think that abundance is a sign of love and scarcity a sign of rejection. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report, citing Qatada and others, that the 'privileged' are the wealthy and leaders who reject the messengers, and that the verse consoles the Prophet ﷺ. Al-Razi holds that the breadth or narrowness of worldly provision does not reveal the state of the righteous or the wrongdoer. Al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Tabari explain that 'yaqdiru' means to restrict, a doubled reading also being transmitted, with the same sense. All agree that nearness to God is gained through faith and good deeds, not through wealth or children, and that whoever spends in God's way will be replaced. They differ on the form of the replacement: according to Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid it means spending without extravagance or stinginess; according to al-Suddi it is the reward in the Hereafter; according to Ibn al-Sa'ib and others it may come in this world or be deferred to the next.

This verse teaches that wealth and children do not bring a person closer to God; only faith and righteous deeds do, and believers will receive multiplied reward and live in security in the lofty chambers of Paradise. The commentators agree that abundance of property and offspring is not proof of divine approval. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi report that the wealthy of Mecca boasted of their riches, and God answers that the expansion or restriction of provision is a test, not a sign of pleasure or anger. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that zulfa means nearness. On the exception 'except those who believe', al-Zajjaj regards it as a substitute for the pronoun in 'brings you near', while al-Farra' treats it as a nominative; Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari read it as an exception meaning 'but', and al-Tabari adds that wealth and children may bring their owner near when spent in God's cause and when children are raised righteously, a view also held by al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi. On the meaning of the multiplication, Ibn Zayd gives ten times for a good deed and seven hundred for spending in God's path, Muhammad ibn Ka'b takes it as a double reward for a pious rich believer, and others understand it as multiplication without a fixed limit. As for the chambers, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take the security to be from punishment, while al-Mawardi and al-Nasafi extend it to death, sorrow and sickness. Ibn 'Ashur observes that the verse denies wealth is the measure of nearness to God without denying its usefulness when spent for good.

The commentators explain that this verse describes those who strive against God's signes, seeking to nullify them and thinking they can escape God, and who will be brought to punishment on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand the striving as efforts to annul God's proofs and Book, while Ibn 'Ashur identifies the target chiefly as the polytheists who turn people away from hearing the Quran and slander it. Regarding the phrase "muhdarun", al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take it to mean they will be brought into Hell, whereas al-Razi sees in it an indication of lasting punishment.

The immediate context explains that the expansion and restriction of provision are a test, not a sign of God's approval or anger. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi note that God widens provision for whom He wills and narrows it for whom He wills, and that wealth and children bring no one closer to Him except the believer who does righteous deeds. The commentators also agree that what is spent in good causes is replaced by God, though they differ on the form of that replacement. Sa'id ibn Jubayr says spending without extravagance or stinginess will be replaced, al-Suddi holds the replacement is a reward in the Hereafter, and al-Kalbi says it may be granted in this world or stored for the next. Mujahid warned against reading the verse as a justification for wastefulness, since provision is apportioned.

Opinions also vary on the "ghurafat". Most take them to be the chambers of Paradise, and al-Qurtubi notes the plural reading is the more common one. The promised security is understood as protection from punishment, death, illness and grief. The overall meaning remains clear: faith and righteous deeds bring one near to God, while those who work against His signs will face punishment.

This verse answers the wealthy elite who boasted of their property and children, taking them as proof of God's favour. The Prophet ﷺ is told to say that his Lord extends provision to whom He wills among His servants and restricts it for whom He wills, and that this is a trial rather than a sign of love or anger. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi explain that expansion and restriction follow God's will and wisdom, which most people do not grasp. On the phrase 'whatever you spend, He replaces it', Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Kalbi take it to mean spending in good without extravagance or stinginess, repaid either in this world or in the Hereafter; al-Sudi limits the replacement to the reward to come, while al-Hasan restricts it to this life. Mujahid warns against reading it as a reason to spend everything and remain in need, since provision is apportioned. Al-Zamakhshari sees the replacement as material, or as contentment, or as reward. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi add that spending in disobedience or on needless building has no replacement. Al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi note that every provider is only an intermediary, and that God is the best of providers.

This verse describes the gathering on the Day of Resurrection, when God assembles the polytheists together with those they worshipped and asks the angels whether those people were worshipping them. The commentators, including al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Sa'di, agree that the angels glorify God and disown this worship, and that the question is meant to rebuke the idolaters and end any hope of intercession. As for the jinn who were worshipped, most identify them with the devils who enticed people into this worship and were obeyed, obedience being a form of worship, as al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn Sa'di maintain. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi report that the devils appeared in the form of angels, and al-Zamakhshari adds that jinn entered idol statues. On the phrase « most of them believe in them », opinions differ: al-Razi explains that the angels avoid claiming full knowledge of all disbelievers and that faith belongs to the heart, while al-Mawardi and al-Baydawi take « most » to mean « all ». The verse continues by stating that on that day no one can benefit or harm another, and the wrongdoers are told to taste the Fire they used to deny.

This verse describes the scene of the Day of Resurrection, when God gathers the disbelievers and those they worshipped. He then asks the angels, to rebuke the disbelievers: 'Was it you whom these people used to worship?' The angels glorify God and disown this worship, saying that God alone is their protector and that they never wanted or ordered it. The commentators explain that 'worship' here means obedience: the idolaters obeyed the jinn, meaning the devils, who made the worship of others seem good to them. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan agree that the jinn meant are the devils who misled people, while the angels do not deny knowing that they were worshipped but disassociate themselves from it. Al-Tabari and al-Baghawi understand the angels' disavowal as a statement that they did not consent. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi see the question as a rhetorical device addressed to the angels in order to heap shame on the disbelievers. On the final phrase 'most of them believed in them', al-Razi and Abu Hayyan offer several explanations: 'most' may mean all, or the speakers did not claim to know every heart, since faith is an inner act that only God knows. Ibn 'Ashur notes that some nations did indeed worship the jinn. Ibn Sa'di and Ibn 'Uthaymin read worship here as obedience. The commentators do not choose between these readings.

This verse describes the Day of Resurrection, when no one can bring benefit or harm to another, so the idols and those worshipped besides God cannot help their worshippers. The wrongdoers, meaning those who associated partners with God, are told to taste the Fire they used to deny. Al-Tabari explains that this refers to those who worshipped other than God and placed worship where it did not belong. Al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Atiyya report that when the angels are questioned they disown their worshippers, saying it was the jinn, meaning the devils, who led people to worship them and whom they obeyed. Al-Razi, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi debate who is addressed: some take it as the angels, others the disbelievers themselves, and al-Razi notes that the wording differs from the parallel in Surat al-Sajda. Al-Qurtubi understands benefit as intercession and harm as punishment. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Nasafi and al-Baydawi stress that the matter belongs to God alone on that Day, since it is a house of reward. Ibn Sa'di sees the verse as a humiliation of the polytheists. Al-Razi adds that mentioning benefit causes regret, while mentioning harm shows that worship has no ground. These commentators agree that the verse contains a warning and a rebuke.

This verse describes how the polytheists responded when clear verses of the Quran were recited to them. They said that the reciter was merely a man who wanted to turn them away from what their forefathers worshipped, then called the Quran a fabricated lie, and finally declared it to be plain sorcery. The commentators agree that these three accusations form a progression: first they attack the Prophet ﷺ himself, then the Quran's content as a fabrication, then its very nature as magic. Al-Zamakhshari sees in this phrasing a sign of great denial and anger, and Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note that they rushed to reject the message without reflection. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi explain that "the truth" may refer to prophethood, to Islam or to the Quran, and that the repetition of the verb may point either to its meaning or to its inimitable form. Al-Tabari, Qatada and Ibn Kathir report that no scripture and no warner had come to the Arabs before the Prophet ﷺ, so they had no knowledge to justify their rejection. Al-Mawardi explains that the word mi'shar means a tenth, or a tenth of a tenth, and that the earlier nations were far stronger than the Quraysh. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari conclude that the punishment of past peoples is a warning to the present ones.

This verse says that the Meccan polytheists had received no scripture they could study, and that no warner had come to them before the Prophet ﷺ, so they had no earlier source to lean on when rejecting the Quran. Commentators read it in two main ways. Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi take it to mean that these books gave no support to idolatry and did not contradict the Prophet's message. Qatada, al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi take it to mean that God had sent no book to the Arabs before the Quran and no prophet before Muhammad ﷺ. Ibn Atiyya notes that Isma'il had warned the Arabs, so the point is that no warner had dedicated himself to them as the Prophet did. Al-Razi and Abu Hayyan attach the pronoun to the book and read the verse as denying any scripture given to the Meccans. On the phrase about not reaching a tenth of what the earlier peoples were given, al-Tabari, Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Ibn Zayd refer it to strength, wealth and long life, while al-Mawardi and Ibn al-Jawzi offer readings about gratitude or proof. Most agree that al-mi'shar means one tenth, though al-Mawardi favours a thousandth. The verse ends with a warning: they denied My messengers, so consider how terrible My rejection was.

The commentators explain that this verse consoles the Prophet ﷺ and warns the disbelievers of Quraysh. The phrase 'those before them denied' means that earlier nations, such as 'Ad, Thamud, the people of Noah, Abraham, Lot and Pharaoh, denied their messengers, so Quraysh's denial is nothing new. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Ibn Zayd, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir state that Quraysh did not reach a tenth of the strength, long life, wealth and children given to those peoples, and that this did not protect them when they rejected the messengers, so their punishment was total destruction. On the word mi'shar, most take it to mean a tenth, while al-Mawardi, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Kathir report it as a tenth of a tenth, a thousandth, and al-Mawardi finds this the more apparent since the aim is to stress how small the share is. Al-Nasafi, Ibn 'Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and al-Alusi mention the reverse reading, that the earlier peoples did not reach a tenth of the proof, clarity and guidance God gave Quraysh, which al-Razi prefers because the Qur'an is the most complete and clear scripture and Muhammad the most eloquent messenger. Finally, 'how was My denial' means how was My punishment: the question is rhetorical, meant to magnify the outcome and warn Quraysh that the same fate could befall them.

God commands His Prophet to tell the idolaters of Quraysh that he exhorts them to only one thing: to stand up for God, in pairs or alone, seeking the truth free from desire and partisanship, and then to reflect on the Prophet ﷺ and his message. The commentators agree that such reflection leads to the conclusion that he is not mad, since those who knew him recognized his sound reason and truthfulness. Al-Tabari, Mujahid and Qatada take this one thing to be obedience to God or monotheism, while al-Zamakhshari and Abu al-Su'ud explain standing up as earnestly committing oneself to the truth rather than physically rising, a reading also given by Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi. Regarding the phrase 'in pairs and alone', al-Mawardi, Ibn Qutayba and Abu Hayyan understand it as two people debating or an individual reflecting alone, and al-Zamakhshari adds that crowds cloud judgement and stir up partisanship. Scholars disagree on the grammatical role of 'that you stand up', as a substitute, an appositive or an implied predicate, and Abu Hayyan rejects apposition here. Some link 'there is no madness in your companion' to the act of reflection, while others treat it as a separate statement. Most read 'warner' as a warning of the punishment of the Hereafter, though Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn also include worldly punishment. Other commentators, such as Ibn Ashur, emphasize the progression from denying madness to affirming his prophetic mission.

God tells His Prophet to say to the polytheists that he asks them for no reward for his call and warning. If he had asked for anything, it would be theirs, and his true reward is with God alone, who witnesses all things and knows his sincerity. Most commentators understand the reward as material payment: Qatada, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi state that the Prophet asked them for nothing in return for delivering the message. Ibn Abbas, as reported by al-Mawardi, Ibn Juzayy and al-Alusi, takes it to mean the affection owed to kin, which benefits those who give it. Al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud read the phrase as a total denial of any request, as if to say that whatever he had asked of them would be theirs, which in effect denies that he asked anything at all.

On the meaning of the witness, al-Mawardi gives two readings: that God witnesses the Prophet is not mad, and that he is a warner before a severe punishment. Ibn Kathir takes it as God's knowledge of the true state of every person. The following verses, which the commentators connect to this one, say that God casts down the truth, that the truth has come, and that falsehood neither originates nor returns. Qatada links falsehood to Satan, al-Dahhak to the idols, and others to error itself, which vanishes with the truth. Finally, one who strays harms only himself, and one who is guided owes it to God's revelation.

God commands His Prophet to tell the idolaters of his people that his Lord casts the truth, that is the revelation, upon whomever He chooses among His servants, and that He is the Knower of the unseen, nothing being hidden from Him. Most commentators, including al-Tabari, Qatada, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi, understand the truth as the revelation and the Quran, and the verb qadhafa as meaning to cast down or send to the prophets. Ibn Zayd, in one of al-Tabari's reports, along with al-Baydawi and Ibn 'Ashur, read it as hurling the truth against falsehood to crush it, a sense also noted by al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi. On grammar, those who read 'Allam in the nominative treat it as a second predicate or an appositive, while those who read it in the accusative take it as a qualifier or a form of praise, and some readers vary the vowel of al-ghuyub. The following verse says the truth has come and falsehood can neither begin nor return, which Ibn Kathir, al-Shawkani and al-Jaza'iri take to mean that falsehood has vanished without a trace. As to what the falsehood is, Qatada and al-Suddi identify it with Iblis, al-Dahhak with the idols, while al-Mawardi, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi also allow it to mean falsehood in general or polytheism.

God tells His Prophet to say: the Truth has come, meaning the Revelation, the Qur'an and Islam, and falsehood has vanished, so that it neither begins anything nor restores anything. The commentators explain that truth has appeared and been established, while error has perished and left no trace, no word and no power to originate or to bring back. They take this from the image of a living being: once it dies, it can no longer begin or repeat anything, so the phrase becomes a figure of speech for complete annihilation, as in the verse of 'Ubayd ibn al-Abras. Al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Ibn Kathir adopt this meaning and cite the report, found in the two Sahihs, of the Prophet striking the idols with a stick while reciting the verse. On the identity of falsehood, opinions differ: Qatada, Muqatil and al-Kalbi identify it with Iblis, who creates and resurrects no one, al-Dahhak with the idols, and Ibn Bahr with the religion of polytheism. al-Hasan reads it as meaning that it brings no good to its people in this world or the next. Al-Zajjaj and others take 'ma' as an interrogative, which amounts to a negation. al-Zamakhshari, al-Baydawi and al-Qasimi see the verse as confirming that God hurls the truth against falsehood to crush it.

God instructs His Prophet to tell the disbelievers that if he has gone astray, as they claim, the burden of that error falls on him alone, and if he is rightly guided, it is by what his Lord reveals to him. Commentators agree that the verse answers the Meccans' charge that he had abandoned the religion of his fathers. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi all read it as a clear division: going astray is one's own responsibility, while guidance comes from God through revelation. Al-Zamakhshari explains that attributing error to the self is a general rule for every responsible person, and that the Prophet was told to say it of himself out of humility, since anyone else would be even more accountable. Al-Razi adds that the Prophet's error would be like that of others, since it would come from his own soul, whereas his guidance does not rest on reasoning as theirs does but on clear revelation. As for the closing words, al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir take them to mean that God hears what His servants say and answers those who call upon Him, while Ibn Juzayy, al-Baydawi and Abu al-Su'ud understand nearness as God's knowledge and encompassing presence. On the reading of the verb, al-Hasan and Ibn Wathhab recite it with a kasra on the first letter, a dialect form attributed to the tribe of Tamim, while the majority read it with a fatha.

This verse describes the terror of the disbelievers when they are seized and cannot escape, and their belated wish to believe. The commentators differ on when this terror occurs. Al-Tabari, followed by Ibn Kathir, holds that it is a warning to the polytheists who rejected the Prophet, with the terror coming when they witness punishment, though Ibn Kathir considers the Day of Resurrection the more sound meaning. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak take it as the punishment of this world, while al-Hasan and Qatada place the terror at the moment of rising from the graves. Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi attribute it to the polytheists slain at Badr, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr reports, through narrations Ibn Kathir judges weak, the swallowing of an army in the desert. As for being seized from a near place, some say from beneath their feet, others from the place of standing to the Fire, others from the surface of the earth to its inside. The word tanawush, meaning to reach for what is far, is taken by some as a plea to return to the world, by others as repentance, and by all as a hope that has become impossible. The phrase qadhf bil-ghayb, hurling words without knowledge, refers to their charges against the Prophet of being a poet, sorcerer, soothsayer or madman, and to their denial of resurrection, reward and the Fire.

This verse describes the state of the disbelievers when they see the punishment: they say, "We believe in it," meaning in God, His Book and His Messenger according to some commentators, or in the Resurrection and the Qur'an according to others. The verse, however, regards it as unlikely that they can reach faith when they are in the Hereafter, where the time for action has ended. Most commentators therefore understand the question "how can they reach it?" as asking how they could obtain faith, repentance or a return to the world once the time for them has passed. The word "at-tanawush" is a known linguistic point. Most readers pronounce it without a hamza, meaning to reach or take hold of, while Abu 'Amr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a hamza, meaning to delay or be late. Some hold that the two readings are close in meaning. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada take it as reaching or returning, al-Suddi as repentance, and al-Hasan as seeking what cannot be attained. As for "from a distant place", some take it to mean from the Hereafter to this world, while al-Zamakhshari reads it as an image of seeking what cannot happen. The time of the terror is also disputed. Mujahid and most commentators say it is the Day of Resurrection, Qatada the moment of rising from the graves, Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak the punishment of this world, and al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd the battle of Badr. Ibn Kathir holds the Day of Resurrection to be the correct view. The common thread is that the faith that no longer helps is the faith that comes after seeing the punishment, from people who had rejected the message and slandered the Prophet with baseless words.

This passage describes the state of the disbelievers on the Day of Judgment or when punishment reaches them. They rejected what they were called to in this life, and they hurled accusations at the truth from a far place, which the commentators read as speaking without knowledge. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi agree that the denial concerned God, the resurrection, the Prophet or the Qur'an, depending on the view. Al-Hasan and Qatada take the hurling in the dark to mean claiming there is no resurrection, no Paradise and no Fire. Mujahid says it refers to calling the Prophet a magician, poet or soothsayer, and Ibn Zayd says it refers to attacks on the Qur'an. Al-Zamakhshari explains the distant place as the great distance between such claims and the truth, while al-Razi links it to the gap between this world and the next. On the word tanawush, most explain it as reaching for something, and the hamza reading as meaning to be late, so their faith comes too late. The scholars differ on what was withheld from them: faith according to al-Hasan, repentance according to al-Suddi, return to the world according to Ibn Abbas, or worldly pleasures according to Mujahid. Finally, the troubling doubt is understood as a doubt that causes unease and suspicion.

This verse describes the state of the disbelievers when they witness the punishment: they are prevented from obtaining what they desire, namely an accepted faith and deliverance, just as was done to their counterparts among earlier peoples, because they were in a doubt that breeds unease. The commentators differ on what they desired. Al-Hasan and Qatada take it to mean faith, obedience to God and the acceptance of repentance, while Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and others take it to mean wealth, family, children and the pleasures of this world. Ibn Abbas and others take it to mean a return to the life of this world. Ibn Kathir sees no contradiction between these views, since they were barred both from worldly pleasures and from what they sought in the Hereafter.

They also differ on who the "counterparts" are. Muqatil says they are the earlier nations, al-Dahhak the people of the elephant, and al-Hasan and Qatada the disbelievers of past nations. As for the "troubling doubt", Muqatil explains it as their failure to recognise their prophet, al-Dahhak as their doubt that the punishment would come, while al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and others understand it as a doubt that provokes suspicion and unease. Qatada reads it as a warning against doubt.

The word "tanawush" is read with or without a hamza depending on the reciter. Ibn Abbas and Ibn Kathir understand it as seeking a return to the world, while al-Hasan and Qatada understand it as grasping at faith when it no longer benefits.
